title: Traditional Honey Meat Roast
community: Multiple communities — Central Kenya and Rift Valley
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: Multiple Kenyan communities — particularly Central Kenya (Kikuyu, Embu, Meru) and Rift Valley
heritage.history: Honey has been harvested and used in Kenyan cooking for thousands of years. Many Kenyan communities — particularly forest-adjacent communities in Central Kenya — have a tradition of using wild honey as a marinade and glaze for roasted meat. Beekeeping remains an important tradition in Meru, Embu, and other Central Kenya communities.
heritage.modernEvolution: Honey-glazed meat is experiencing a revival as interest in indigenous ingredients and traditional preparations grows.

desc: Traditional Honey Meat Roast — large cuts of beef or goat marinated in wild Kenyan honey, garlic, and herbs, then slow-roasted over charcoal until the honey caramelises into a magnificent dark, fragrant crust. The most celebratory indigenous Kenyan roasting tradition.
longDesc: Honey meat roast is Kenya at its most primordial and most delicious — raw honey from forest hives applied to fresh meat and held over fire until it caramelises into something extraordinary.
ingredients: 2 kg bone-in goat shoulder or beef chuck — scored deeply
6 tbsp raw wild honey — preferably Kenyan forest honey
steps: Score the meat deeply all over — 4—5 cuts per surface, to the bone.
Combine honey, garlic, lemon juice, ginger, salt, pepper, oil, and coriander.
Rub the honey marinade thoroughly all over and deep into the scores.
Marinate for a minimum of 2 hours — overnight is best.
Prepare charcoal to glowing coals — medium heat.
Place meat over medium indirect heat — not directly over coals.
Roast for 75—90 minutes, turning every 20 minutes.
In the final 20 minutes, move to direct heat and baste every 5 minutes.
chefTips: Wild honey is essential — the complex floral character creates a completely different result from processed honey.
Watch carefully in the final 20 minutes — honey burns quickly over direct heat.
Overnight marination allows the honey to penetrate deeply.
commonMistakes: Starting with direct heat — the honey burns before the interior is cooked.

faqs.q: Where can I find wild Kenyan honey?
faqs.a: Wild Kenyan forest honey is available from artisanal beekeepers in Central Kenya (Meru, Embu, Nyeri), the Taita Hills, and increasingly in Nairobi specialty food markets.

cookingScience: Honey contains approximately 80% sugars that caramelise between 150—170°C, creating hundreds of new flavour compounds. Fructose caramelises at a lower temperature than sucrose — making honey brown more rapidly than table sugar.
sustainabilityTips: Supporting artisanal Kenyan beekeepers sustains biodiversity and traditional forest management.
storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 3 days.
reheating: Reheat on grill for best result.
healthBenefits: Wild honey provides antioxidants and natural antimicrobials.
Garlic and ginger add anti-inflammatory benefits.
culturalNote: Traditional honey meat roast represents a cross-community Kenyan culinary tradition as old as beekeeping itself — a reminder that food has always been a bridge between cultures.
